# What Quarto is, and why bother {#sec-what}

Quarto is a free, open-source publishing system. You write in plain text —
`.qmd` files, which are Markdown plus optional live code — and Quarto renders
that same source into a website, a book, a PDF, slides, or a Word document.

If you have used R Markdown, this is its successor: the same idea, grown up and
no longer tied to R.

## Why it suits teaching

**Everything is text.** Your book is a folder of readable files. It fits in
Git, it diffs sensibly, and a colleague can open it in any editor.

**Maths renders properly.** LaTeX between dollar signs, in the browser and on
paper, from one source.

**Code can run.** A plot in your reader can be generated by the code that
produced it, so the figure and the analysis never drift apart.

**Simulations sit next to the explanation.** A student can read the model and
then immediately turn its knobs — see @sec-iframes. And with @sec-webr they can
edit your R or Python and run it, in the browser, with nothing installed. This
is the part that really pays off.

**Structure comes free.** Sidebar, search box, chapter numbering,
cross-references and a table of contents are all generated for you.

The [quarto.org](https://quarto.org) gallery page, and side by side a `.qmd`
source file next to its rendered HTML output.

## What you need to install

Three things, in this order.

1. **[R](https://cran.r-project.org)** — the language.
2. **[RStudio Desktop](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/)** — the
   editor. RStudio v2022.07 and later has built-in Quarto support.
3. **[Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/)** — the publishing system.

Recent RStudio versions ship with a copy of Quarto bundled, so step 3 is
sometimes optional. Install it separately anyway: it means you know which
version you have, and can say so to a colleague.

Restart RStudio after installing Quarto so it notices.

::: {.callout-note}
## Which version am I on?
In RStudio: <kbd>Tools</kbd> → <kbd>Terminal</kbd> → <kbd>New Terminal</kbd>,
then type `quarto --version`. This is the only time in this guide you need a
terminal, and you can skip it if you would rather not.
:::

::: {.screenshot}
RStudio's *About* screen showing the bundled Quarto version, and a terminal
showing `quarto --version`.
:::

## Document, website, or book?

One file — `_quarto.yml` at the top of your folder — decides what you are
building.

| `type:` | What you get | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| `default` | A single standalone document | A hand-out, a practical, one lecture |
| `website` | Many pages with a top navigation bar | A course site: schedule, links, materials |
| `book` | Numbered chapters, a sidebar, cross-references, and a combined PDF | A course reader |

A book *is* a website with extra structure, so starting as a website and
graduating to a book later costs almost nothing. This guide assumes a book.

## Not an R user? {#sec-other-languages}

Almost nothing here is really about R. Write ```` ```{python} ```` instead
of ```` ```{r} ```` and your code chunks run Python; Julia and Observable JS
work too, and a book can mix them. If your book is entirely Python, set
`engine: jupyter` in `_quarto.yml`.

Everything else — the structure, the figures, the callouts, the iframes, the
publishing — is identical whichever language you use, and identical whether you
edit in RStudio, VS Code, Positron or a plain text editor.
